findings: THE COLLECTION HELD. The excavators and their years, the EES as owner, Oxford as host and 'the largest archive of its kind in the world' are the record's ('Grenfell and Arthur Hunt in 1896–1907 on behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund (now Society)', 'belonging to the Egypt Exploration Society and housed in Oxford's Art, Archaeology and Ancient World Library', the largest of its kind). Checked 2026-10-31 against the Revelation First census record of 2026-10-30 and the sources it saved.

THE RANGE: THE OPERATOR'S TWO PAGES DISAGREE. 'The texts date from the 3rd century BCE (Ptolemaic period) through the 7th century CE'. The collection's Oxford page (card 1): 'dating from the second century BCE to the seventh century CE'. The Egypt Exploration Society's own page (card 3): 'over 500,000 fragments of literary and documentary texts dating from the third century BCE to the seventh century CE', as the Wikipedia card has it ('3rd century BC to 640 AD'). The composition follows the EES and Wikipedia and does not note the difference.

PAPYRUS 52 AMONG THE FINDS. 'biblical fragments (such as Papyrus 52 and the Gospel of Thomas)'. Papyrus 52 is the Rylands fragment of John (P.Ryl. Gr. 457, John Rylands Library, Manchester), bought in Egypt in 1920 with no recorded findspot; it has no number in the Oxyrhynchus series. The Thomas fragments do (P.Oxy. 1, 654 and 655). The record's does_not_answer is exactly this: which New Testament papyri the collection holds is not on the saved page.
A FIGURE FROM THE EES CARD. 'an estimated 500,000 fragments' is the EES page's (card 3: 'over 500,000 fragments'); the census's saved Oxford page says 'thousands of texts'.

THE NEGATIVE TAG KEPT IN SUBSTANCE. The record keeps the collection apart from a New Testament collection; the composition's '90%' of documents and '10%' literary and religious says the same at its own grain.

[[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVWTfiKDhi_GJUj_uCo4kUTMWJJXuVSBQUu_Lg7Xas6cMOsaeYL9aDLy_7Jt2NwHGqf99n5gM4jYe68B1BQT0NTj1hYis8EJ5-zVK9I8hr9HFxQ7v5dLbddg), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVHKYeH9MMOplsy2m6M44I_4dCdnkJnBpHYOOwiByTHyQ4i_srIQAehR0skIX88lDj2lRGXN1jGRnbOlgKOBEQHQYTsDWaMSohG_vs1oDa7QMj2izXiybQ-EGriN_4cGfTQlCl)]
Key Facts

* The Collection: Housed primarily at the University of Oxford and managed by the [Egypt Exploration Society (EES)](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVE-J-BtE30aDuAYi0uEyXPmirrIaBMLmyKzpD07kyURlmolMbCscrpm40yzKQJKL7O40kms8UP2V7SedqBYyQjJ4_UJOsZZId4RrYO6yNyeJRCPkvRkVZygiyzBuffcQq), it is the largest archive of its kind in the world, containing an estimated 500,000 fragments. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAV1fJTkWvepNpdXcz1FTiTgD2TzJwnIKqlxQFWjqxxST5AeBjCcgJmhPj-Yeh05uZsMeRxIHIalxaCwxJ87W6W-qZRqSMOxT4Ur_-Oy_ULiJ4bJ0OVBS0Zjyw_aPuj2G39H4nt)]
* Languages: Most texts are in Greek, with others written in Latin, ancient Egyptian, Coptic, Arabic, Hebrew, and Aramaic. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAV1fJTkWvepNpdXcz1FTiTgD2TzJwnIKqlxQFWjqxxST5AeBjCcgJmhPj-Yeh05uZsMeRxIHIalxaCwxJ87W6W-qZRqSMOxT4Ur_-Oy_ULiJ4bJ0OVBS0Zjyw_aPuj2G39H4nt), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZQHrOzAVE-J-BtE30aDuAYi0uEyXPmirrIaBMLmyKzpD07kyURlmolMbCscrpm40yzKQJKL7O40kms8UP2V7SedqBYyQjJ4_UJOsZZId4RrYO6yNyeJRCPkvRkVZygiyzBuffcQq)]
